This document describes how birdMonitor turns bird records and environmental data into yearly occurrence maps and national and regional indices, with confidence intervals, for the breeding bird species of the roster in Germany from 2005 to 2025. *Note of 29 October 2026: the method does not depend on the number of species (the roster can grow or shrink); the numbers in the text are those of the runs of 12 and 13 October, which had 11 species. The changes made since then, which apply from the clean run for the first version of the Monitor (14 species), are listed in section 9. Note of 5 November 2026: the descriptions of the method follow the code of that clean run (14 species, big 5 only, 25 replicates, 90% intervals); numbers that come from the 11-species runs are labelled as such.*

## 1. Overview

The pipeline follows the multi-scale meta-model approach of Wiedenroth et al. (preprint, 2026) and adds honest weighting, an uncertainty framework and an algorithm ensemble.

1. **Data preparation.** Bird records of three kinds, one per spatial scale, are cleaned and thinned, and matched to climate, landscape and habitat layers.
2. **One model per scale.** A boosted regression tree is fitted at the climate scale (50 km), the landscape scale (1 km) and the habitat scale (200 m), with spatial block cross-validation.
3. **Meta-model.** A ridge regression combines the three scale predictions into one probability of occurrence per 200 m pixel and year.
4. **Indices and maps.** From these yearly maps we compute species indices, three combined indices (SBI, MSI and Chain), change and gain-loss maps, expected richness, turnover, and regional indices on 10, 20 and 50 km grids.
5. **Uncertainty.** Steps 2 and 3 are repeated on spatial bootstrap resamples of the training data, and every product of step 4 is recomputed inside each replicate.
6. **Big 5.** In step 2, the single algorithm at each scale is replaced by five algorithms (BRT, GLM, GAM, random forest, neural network) whose predictions are averaged within that scale. The meta-model of step 3 then combines the three scale averages, and steps 3 to 5 are repeated, with their own uncertainty. The first version of the Monitor (14 species) is run in this form only: the BRT is one of the five members, and the uncertainty run has 25 replicates.

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Species | Those marked `include` in `data/speciesCanonical.csv`; the table holds 17 species, 14 of them on in the first version of the Monitor (Alauda arvensis, Anthus pratensis, Buteo buteo, Curruca communis, Emberiza calandra, Emberiza citrinella, Falco tinnunculus, Lanius collurio, Lullula arborea, Motacilla flava, Passer montanus, Saxicola rubetra, Sturnus vulgaris, Vanellus vanellus). The runs of 12 and 13 October, whose numbers are in this document, had 11 (the same without Curruca communis, Falco tinnunculus, Motacilla flava and Passer montanus, and with Perdix perdix). Perdix perdix, Streptopelia turtur and Milvus milvus are off |
| Years mapped | 2005 to 2025 (21); baseline year 2005 |
| Scales | climate 50 km, landscape 1 km, habitat 200 m |
| Final grid | 200 m pixels in the EPSG:3035 projection |
| Computation | UFZ cluster EVE, R with SpaDES modules |

## 2. Data

Each scale has its own bird data and its own environmental layers, and the three scales are combined only at the meta-model step.

| Scale | Bird data | Environmental layers | Years of bird training (model fitting) data |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Climate, 50 km | EBBA2 breeding-bird atlas, 50 km grid | CHELSA bioclimatic variables, summarised in six-year windows (the window of year Y covers Y-5 to Y; the 2025 window has data to September only) | One climate window, 2012-2017, for all atlas records. The model then predicts every year from 2005 to 2025 from the window ending in that year |
| Landscape, 1 km | DDA territory mapping (BirdStats 2005-2024); for Buteo buteo and Sturnus vulgaris the MhB point counts instead | Land-use fractions, terrain, woodland distance, landscape heterogeneity | 2005-2024 for the DDA species; 2022-2025 for Buteo buteo and Sturnus vulgaris. The model predicts 2025 for the DDA species too, so 2025 is a forecast at this scale |
| Habitat, 200 m | MhB (Monitoring haeufiger Brutvoegel) point counts along the survey routes | The same kind of layers at 200 m, plus hedges for the species that use them | 2022-2025 only. The model then predicts every year from 2005 to 2025 at this scale |

Two species have another landscape resolution than 1 km: Lanius collurio (700 m) and Buteo buteo (5 km).

**Environmental layers.** The land-use layers are fractions of crops (winter and summer cereals, maize, rapeseed, root crops, legumes, sunflower, vegetables, orchards, vines, hops), fallow, grassland, trees, water and built-up area; terrain is elevation and slope. Which of these enter a species' model is set in a configuration table per species and scale. At the climate scale every species starts from all 19 bioclimatic variables. They are strongly correlated and are not pruned for the GLM, the GAM or the neural network, which may make those models less stable outside the range of the training data, as in the hindcast. We have not tested a pruned set. The hedge layer is one fixed layer, the mean of the hedge layers of all years that have hedge data (since 3 November 2026), so hedges give no change over time.

**Preparing the records.** The four data sources (DDA territories, MhB at two scales, EBBA2) do not record absences in the same way, so each builds its presences and absences differently. No absences are drawn at random from the background; they all come from the survey data. But for MhB (at both scales) and EBBA2 a site counts as surveyed only by inference, not by a record of the visit. The table gives the rule per scale.

| Scale and data | Presence | Absence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Habitat, MhB point counts | A detection between April and June, with a count above zero and an accepted breeding code; one presence per 200 m cell and year | A route-year counts as surveyed if at least one species of the roster has a qualifying record on it that year (MhB has no log of visits without a detection). The absence is the centre of the survey polygon of a surveyed route where the species has no qualifying record that year, if the 200 m cell has data and is not a presence cell. Inferred, not recorded |
| Landscape, DDA territories (all species except Buteo buteo and Sturnus vulgaris) | A visited route-year with a territory count above zero, or with a count of -1 (seen, not counted). No month filter and no breeding code apply | A visited route-year of the DDA visits list without such a count. Recorded, as the visits list says which routes were visited |
| Landscape, MhB (Buteo buteo and Sturnus vulgaris) | A qualifying record (April to June, accepted code) at the route in that year, aggregated to the route; Buteo buteo needs confirmed breeding (C) | A route-year counts as surveyed if any species in the MhB file, not only the roster, has a qualifying record on it. Absence = surveyed route without the species. Inferred; the surveyed rule is wider than at the habitat scale, and no count filter is applied |
| Climate, EBBA2 | A 50 km atlas square where the species is recorded | The extract lists presences only. A square counts as surveyed if at least one of the 17 species of the extract is recorded there, and the species is absent in such a square where it is not recorded. Squares where none of the 17 occurs never become absences. Inferred; the absences depend on the species list of the extract and grew when species were added |

The MhB records carry the code of the German atlas system (`ATLAS_CODE`), which distinguishes possible (A), probable (B) and confirmed (C) breeding. We keep every code except the weakest one, a bare "A" without a number. The bird records are filtered to the breeding season (April to June) only in the MhB branches; the DDA and EBBA2 data are used as they come. A species recorded at an MhB route only before April counts as absent there, which can matter for early breeders such as Vanellus vanellus, Lullula arborea and Buteo buteo, and the scales therefore differ in season. Presences and absences are thinned together by a species-specific distance, so that dense survey areas do not dominate. The distance is 100 km at the climate scale, 400 m at the habitat scale and 2 km at the landscape scale (1.4 km for Lanius collurio and 10 km for Buteo buteo there). At the landscape and habitat scales the records are matched to the layers of the year they were collected in; the climate records use the single window 2012-2017.

**Spatial blocks.** The records of each scale are grouped into spatial blocks, five folds of them, whose size comes from the range of spatial autocorrelation that `blockCV::cv_spatial_autocor()` finds. The call receives the presence-absence records (the column `occurrence`) and no predictor layers, so, as far as we can tell from the code, the range refers to the response and not to the predictors; we have not checked this against the installed version of `blockCV`. The range is capped at 1500 km at the climate scale and at 200 km at the other two, and floored at 200 km at the climate scale and at twice the resolution at the other two. The blocks are used for cross-validation. The bootstrap (section 7) uses a square grid of blocks whose size is derived in the same way.

**Why the habitat scale has only four years.** By a project decision, MhB point counts are used only from 2022: earlier MhB records are inconsistent and were collected with a different method (the raw record counts are small before 2020 and jump from 2020). For 2005-2021 the habitat model is therefore applied to older layers as a hindcast (see section 8).

## 3. Models

Each scale gets its own model, and a meta-model then learns how much to trust each scale.

**Scale models.** At each scale a boosted regression tree (BRT, `gbm`) predicts the probability of occurrence from that scale's predictors. The number of trees is chosen by the internal cross-validation of the fitting routine, which uses random folds, not spatial blocks. The number of trees, the learning rate, the tree complexity and the bag fraction of the main fit are then kept fixed in every cross-validation fold and in every bootstrap replicate. Accuracy is measured by five-fold spatial block cross-validation: each fold holds out whole blocks, so a record is never tested against its own neighbours. Because the tree count and the learning rate were chosen on all records before this cross-validation, the accuracy is somewhat optimistic; we do not know by how much. The fold models are saved, because they supply the out-of-fold predictions used afterwards (i.e., see below).

**Meta-model.** The three scale predictions at the habitat records are combined by a logistic ridge regression (`glmnet`). The coefficients are constrained to be zero or positive, so a scale can only add evidence. The penalty is chosen by cross-validation (ten random folds, in the main model and in every bootstrap replicate), as the largest penalty within one standard error of the best one (`lambda.1se`). The meta-model is fitted on the habitat records of 2022-2025, pooled, and is then applied to every 200 m pixel and year, which gives the yearly probability maps that all indices are built from. **Important note on a previous attempt:** replicates first used spatial block folds, which are stricter. However, these shrank the weights and the trends, so that version is kept as a sensitivity analysis (the switch `BIRDMONITOR_UNC_RIDGEFOLDS=block`) but should not be interpreted as the correct approach. The size of the trend depends on this rule: in the BRT-only run the replicate mean of the combined index in 2025 was 97.5 with block folds and 96.1 with random folds, against 95.6 for the main model. Random folds have their own weak point. The records of a replicate contain some blocks twice, so copies of one record can sit on both sides of a split, and the penalty may then be too small. The comparison of the penalties of the replicates with the penalty of the main model is still to be done on the v3 results.

**Why the weights are honest.** The inputs to the meta-model are out-of-fold predictions: each habitat record is predicted by a scale model that did not see the record's block. This is exact at the habitat scale. At the climate and landscape scales the blocks of the habitat records were not saved. The record gets the fold of the nearest record of that scale's own training table and is predicted by that fold's model. Near a block border the nearest record can belong to another fold, so the nesting is approximate, and at the 50 km climate scale the nearest record can be far from the habitat record. We have not measured the effect on the weights. The fold models are refitted with the specification chosen on all records: the GLM terms, the number of trees and the forest and network settings stay fixed. The GAM tries its stored settings first and uses its fallback settings only if they fail. The selection therefore saw the held-out blocks, and the out-of-fold predictions are mildly optimistic, probably most for the GLM, whose terms were chosen by AIC. The accuracy of the meta-model is evaluated on the same out-of-fold inputs. The evaluation is a nested cross-validation. The outer folds are the spatial blocks of the habitat records, and inside each the penalty is chosen with five random folds, whereas the final weights use ten. The reported AUC is therefore that of a slightly different procedure than the one that produced the weights. This is different from what Wiedenroth et al., developed, whose weights are fitted on in-sample predictions. We believe that this is why our accuracy figures are lower, but still more trustworthy. The switch `metaHonestEval` (default TRUE, as in the first version of the Monitor) controls this. With FALSE the ridge is fitted on in-sample inputs, which changes the weights, every map and every index built from the maps, and not only the reported accuracy.

**What the accuracy and the weights say.** In the BRT-only run of 12 October the honest AUC of the meta-model lies between 0.71 (Buteo buteo) and 0.95 (for example Alauda arvensis). The climate scale has a positive weight for 10 of the 11 species and weight zero for Emberiza calandra. With the big 5 the AUC lies between 0.726 and 0.958 (handover document, section 7.5). In the big 5 run, the AUC of the meta-model is below the AUC of its own habitat input for Vanellus vanellus (0.865 against 0.940) and, marginally, for Buteo buteo (0.726 against 0.728). A combination that contains the habitat input should rarely be worse than it. Possible causes are other record sets (complete cases of the three inputs), the nearest-fold approximation and the number of inner folds; we have not tested them, and we will look at this in the v3 results. The AUC describes how well held-out blocks of 2022-2025 are predicted. It says nothing about the hindcast years. The weights are coefficients on probabilities, not shares, and the three scale predictions are correlated, so a weight cannot be read as the contribution of a scale. The same holds for the importance of a scale that the pipeline saves (the drop in explained deviance when the scale is left out, computed in-sample at the fixed penalty): it understates scales whose information the others share, and we use it for ranking only. Accuracy of the three scale models is not comparable across scales, because each is tested on different records.

**Binary maps.** The binary maps are an addition at the very end of the chain. Everything is computed on probabilities, and only once the probability map of a year exists do we derive a presence-absence map from it: a species is called present in a pixel when its probability reaches a threshold chosen per species from the same honest evaluation. The threshold is the one that maximises sensitivity plus specificity on the out-of-fold predictions. It therefore depends on the ratio of presences to absences among the surveyed route-years and not on the prevalence of the species in Germany, and it can over-call presence for rare species. The accuracy measures that need a threshold (TSS, sensitivity, specificity) are computed at the threshold that maximises them on the same predictions and are optimistic; the AUC needs no threshold. One threshold per species is applied to all 21 years, so gains and losses between the hindcast years and 2025 partly reflect a fixed cut-off being crossed. The binary maps feed the gain-and-loss maps, the counts of gained and lost species, the richness map built from binary maps (`SR_binary`) and the presence-absence figures; the indices, the change in probability, the expected richness and the turnover all use the probabilities themselves.

**Years.** The habitat scale is trained on 2022-2025, the landscape scale on 2005-2024 (Buteo buteo and Sturnus vulgaris: 2022-2025) and the climate scale on one climate window (2012-2017). The meta-model is trained on the habitat years. All three scales (via the meta-model) predict all 21 years; the further a year is from the habitat years, the more the result is a hindcast. The weights of the three scales are fitted on four years and are assumed to hold for all 21. This is not tested; a temporal hold-out is still to be done (improvements.md, item 10).

## 4. The big 5 ensemble

The big 5 replaces the single boosted regression tree at each scale by five algorithms, so that no single algorithm decides the result. The order of the steps matters. First, at each of the three scales separately, the five algorithms are fitted and their five predictions are averaged into one ensemble prediction for that scale. The honest ridge meta-model of section 3 then combines the three scale ensembles into the probability of occurrence, exactly as it combined the three BRT predictions before. Averaging across the big 5 therefore happens within each scale; the ridge meta-model then combines the three scale ensembles. There is one meta-model per species (and one per bootstrap replicate), not one per algorithm. This is the design of Wiedenroth et al., who chose it for interpretability, and it also means that we fit one meta-model instead of five.

| Member | How it is fitted |
| --- | --- |
| BRT | Boosted regression tree, as in section 3 |
| GLM | Logistic regression with linear and quadratic terms, selected by AIC (as in Wiedenroth et al.) |
| GAM | Logistic additive model (`mgcv`) with one smooth per predictor (`s(x, k = 4)`, at most three effective degrees of freedom); if the default fit does not converge, more robust settings are tried before any predictor is dropped (REML with more iterations, then the extended Fellner-Schall optimiser, then k = 3, and only then the sparsest predictor is dropped). In a cross-validation fold or a replicate the stored settings are tried first, and the same ladder is used if they fail. A GAM that needed one of these fallbacks is a simpler or differently estimated model than the plain description, still a valid fit; each fit records which setting was used, and `tools/countAlgoFallbacks.R` lists the species and scales concerned after a run (count for v3: to be added) |
| Random forest | `ranger`, 1000 trees, one third of the predictors tried at each split, minimum node size 5, grown as a regression forest on the 0/1 response, so the prediction is the mean of the trees (the published work used `randomForest`; `ranger` is much faster with the same defaults) |
| Neural network | `nnet`, one hidden layer of 3 units, weight decay 0.1, up to 1000 iterations, standardised predictors, the mean of 5 random starts; these settings come from the sensitivity analysis described below |

**One shared design.** All five members start from the same candidate predictors and use the same spatial folds as the BRT of that scale. The GLM can drop terms by AIC, and the GAM can drop a predictor that keeps it from converging. Each member's cross-validated predictions at the habitat records are kept. The ensemble prediction is the arithmetic mean of the five. A model can only predict a pixel where all of its predictor layers have a value. In the runs of 12 and 13 October this is why four species (Emberiza citrinella, Lanius collurio, Lullula arborea and Sturnus vulgaris) had predictions inside Germany only: their models used the hedge and landscape-heterogeneity layers, which, as far as we can tell from the predictor lists, existed for Germany only. For the other seven species the maps covered almost the whole prediction window (the bounding box of Germany). In the clean run for the first version of the Monitor, every layer is cut to the study area and complete inside it (section 9), so all species are predicted over the same area. The five members use the same candidate predictors, so they all have a prediction in the same pixels. As a safeguard, a pixel where any member has no prediction is left empty instead of being averaged over fewer members.

**Neural-network settings.** The network is the one member that was not published, so its settings were tested before use: nine combinations of 3, 10 and 20 hidden units and decay 0.01, 0.1 and 1, at all three scales, under spatial cross-validation (one species, three random starts). The first setting (10 units, 300 iterations) did not converge in 15 of 15 landscape fits. Three units with decay 0.1 matched or beat the best setting at every scale and converged in the pilot. The grid ran 300 iterations, so the final setting with up to 1000 iterations was not run as such. The pilot used the same spatial folds that give the final accuracy, and convergence is not checked in the production fits:

| Scale | AUC, 10 units, decay 0.1 | AUC, 3 units, decay 0.1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Climate | 0.888 | 0.904 |
| Landscape | 0.874 | 0.879 |
| Habitat | 0.938 | 0.940 |

In an earlier local test on one species, the five-member ensemble was more accurate than any single member at the landscape scale (AUC 0.885 against 0.865 to 0.879).

**Uncertainty with the ensemble.** In the bootstrap, every replicate refits all five members on its own resample and trains its own ridge meta-model, so the choice of algorithm adds to the interval instead of being hidden. If a member cannot be refitted on a resample even with its most robust settings (for the GAM: REML, a second optimiser, three knots, then dropping the sparsest predictor), the main fit of that member stands in for that replicate. In such a replicate that member does not vary, so frequent fallbacks narrow the interval; the number of such cases is counted and logged per species, scale and member, but no check stops the run or flags a species when they are frequent. The log is the file `refit_fallbacks.csv` in the `models/` folder of each species in the uncertainty run, and the counts are summarised in the handover document, section 7.3.

## 5. The indices in detail

All indices are built from the yearly probability maps of section 3, and none of them is a count: they are model-based indices of the probability of occurrence, not TRIM indices (which model counts and cannot be applied to probabilities).

**Species index.** For species s and year t, let P(s,t) be the mean probability of occurrence over all pixels inside Germany. The index sets the baseline year 2005 to 100:

$$I_{s,t} = 100 \cdot \frac{P_{s,t}}{P_{s,2005}}$$

**Combined indices.** Three ways of combining the species indices are computed. The SBI and the MSI share the same point estimate in the baseline files, the geometric mean of the species indices (the Swiss Bird Index of Zbinden et al. 2005), and differ only in how the interval is obtained. In the uncertainty files the column `estimate` is not the main-model value: it is the mean over the replicates for the SBI and the Chain index, and the geometric mean of the replicate means of the species indices for the MSI. The report figures draw the main model as the line and the replicate interval as the band. The Chain index is built from year-to-year ratios and gives the same values as the SBI as long as no species is missing in any year.

$$\mathrm{SBI}_t = \exp\left(\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\ln I_{s,t}\right)$$

| Index | Point estimate | Interval | Lineage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SBI | Geometric mean of species indices | Percentile interval over replicates; replicate b of every species is combined (see section 7: the resamples of different species are drawn independently) | Zbinden et al. 2005 |
| MSI | As SBI | Monte Carlo: species indices are drawn from their standard errors, combined, and the percentiles taken | Soldaat et al. 2017, the Monte Carlo step of the MSI method used by the DDA and PECBMS partners; their exclusions and truncation of low values are not implemented here |
| Chain | Geometric mean of year-to-year ratios, cumulated; independent of the baseline year | Percentile interval over replicates | Living Planet Index method |

**Standard error of a species index.** The MSI needs to know how uncertain each species index is, because it builds its interval from that. In the uncertainty run we take it from the bootstrap: for every species and year there is one value of the index per replicate, and their standard deviation is the standard error. There are 25 replicates in the clean run for the first version of the Monitor and there were 50 in the BRT-only run of 12 October. It therefore says how much the index changes when the models are trained on different data. In the baseline run there are no replicates, so the only measure available is spatial: the standard deviation of the probabilities over all pixels of Germany, divided by the square root of the number of pixels. That formula treats every pixel as an independent observation, which they are not (neighbouring pixels are almost identical), and with millions of pixels it gives a very small number. We therefore do not read it as the uncertainty of the index, only as a lower bound, and all intervals we report come from the uncertainty run. The baseline run also writes intervals of its own into the annual-report files: a 95% bootstrap over species for the SBI and the Chain index (columns `lwr95` and `upr95`), and intervals from the pixel-based standard error for the other two. They do not measure model uncertainty and are not the intervals reported here. With no missing species the Chain index equals the SBI; the two diverge only when a species drops out of a year. The baseline run also writes a Chain index restricted to the years with real habitat data (2022-2025), as a robustness check: it shows whether the trend survives when the hindcast years are left out. The setting was the full range 2005-2025 until 5 November, which made the restricted index a copy of the ordinary Chain index. It is now 2022-2025, and the v3 chain (submitted on 5 November, after the change) uses it from the start.

**Smoothing.** Each combined series also has a smoothed version (`SBI_smooth`) for display. The smoothed series is a display of the point estimate and has no interval of its own.

## 6. Maps: change, richness, turnover and the regional index

**Change maps.** For three comparisons, each against the current year (2025): the baseline year 2005, five years earlier (2020) and the previous year (2024). Per pixel and species the map shows the change in probability, a gain-and-loss class from the binary maps (stable absent, loss, gain, stable present), and an increase, decrease or stable class, where a change of more than 0.05 in probability counts as an increase or decrease. The 0.05 is a judgement call and is reported as such. A fixed absolute cut treats a change from 0.06 to 0.01 like one from 0.90 to 0.84. The classes are built so that a change of exactly +0.05 is called stable and exactly -0.05 a decrease; this matters only for values equal to the cut.

**Community layers.** Over all species: `meanDeltaP` (the mean change in probability), `gainCount` and `lossCount` (the number of species crossing the presence threshold upward or downward), `netGainLoss` and `turnoverBC` (below). Expected richness is the sum of the probabilities over the species of the roster, not over the whole community. A species without a prediction in a pixel adds nothing to that pixel. Summing probabilities gives a biased richness unless the probabilities are calibrated, and we have not checked the calibration.

**Turnover.** Richness and the mean change both cancel when species are swapped: five species at probability 0.8 in 2005, four lost and four others gained, gives the same richness and a mean change of zero. The Bray-Curtis dissimilarity between the two years does not cancel:

$$\mathrm{BC} = \frac{\sum_s \left| p_{s,t_1} - p_{s,t_0} \right|}{\sum_s \left( p_{s,t_0} + p_{s,t_1} \right)}$$

It is 0 when the expected community is unchanged and 1 when no species is shared; the swap above gives 0.8. Probabilities stand in for abundances, and the dissimilarity also rises when richness changes without a swap. In the uncertainty run it is computed inside each replicate and summarised by its mean, standard deviation and 90% interval.

**Regional index.** As an example of how our indices can be regionalised, we computed the SBI (the geometric mean of the species indices, section 5) separately for every cell of a 10, 20 or 50 km grid instead of once for the whole country. The cells are blocks of 200 m pixels counted from the corner of the cropped map, not a published reference grid, so they do not coincide with other products' grids. Only the SBI is regionalised; the MSI and the Chain index are not. Everything else is as in section 5, except for three things. First, the 200 m pixels are masked with the German outline before they are averaged into a cell, so a border cell holds pixels from Germany only (a pixel that straddles the border is kept). Second, a species is left out of a cell where its baseline mean is below a floor (currently 10 to the power of minus 6); in the 11-species runs of October no cell came near it (the lowest baseline cell means were above 0.001 and no ratio between 2005 and 2025 exceeded 10; to be checked on the v3 maps), so a higher floor, or a cap on extreme ratios (in the spirit of the truncation of very small index values in Soldaat et al. 2017), is kept as a safeguard rather than needed. Third, a smoothed version applies a Gaussian filter with a standard deviation of 1.5 cells, renormalised at the edges, to the final raw result. The smoothed map has no interval of its own; the raw regional index has one (section 7).

## 7. Uncertainty

The question we ask here is: how different would each result be if the models had been trained on different data? We answer it by refitting the whole chain on resampled data many times. This is a different question from how wrong the environmental layers are, how well the model settings were chosen, how the birds were surveyed, or whether habitat preferences were the same before 2022, none of which this uncertainty covers (see "What is not covered" below).

**The bootstrap.** For each scale, the training records are grouped into square spatial blocks. One replicate draws blocks at random with replacement, as many draws as there are blocks, and takes all records of every block drawn, twice if a block is drawn twice. This is a bootstrap in which the blocks play the role of the independent units, a so-called cluster or block bootstrap. Because blocks differ in size, the number of records differs a little between replicates. The blocks are treated as independent, which is only approximately true because neighbouring blocks are still correlated, so the intervals can be somewhat too narrow. The block grid has a fixed origin, so all replicates share one tessellation and the interval is conditional on it. The three scales and the species are resampled independently of each other. A draw with fewer than 10 presences or 10 absences is redrawn. Each replicate then refits the scale models with the settings of the main fit (nothing is re-tuned), fits its own ridge meta-model on out-of-fold predictions of its own models, predicts all 21 years, and computes every product below inside the replicate. The interval is the 5th to the 95th percentile across replicates (90%). Seeds are fixed per species, scale and replicate and logged, so more replicates can be added later without changing the earlier ones.

**Replicate 0** is the main model run through exactly the same machinery. It is never part of an interval; it checks that the machinery reproduces the baseline maps and indices (the parity check). In the runs of October the valid pixels were the same, the probabilities were equal to within the storage precision of 3.3 x 10^-5 and the area means to about 10^-10. These are observed values, not the criterion. The check compares one band of one year (the current year) per species, and it fails only if the probabilities differ by more than 0.001 or the area mean by more than 0.1 percent. The regional check fails if the 99th percentile of the difference exceeds 0.5 index points. An error in an older year or in another band would not be seen by these checks.

| Product | How the uncertainty enters |
| --- | --- |
| Probability map per year | Mean, standard deviation, 5th and 95th percentile and width of the probability across replicates, per pixel |
| Change maps (three comparisons: 2025 to 2024, 2025 to 2020 and 2025 to 2005) | The change is computed in each replicate; mean, standard deviation, interval, width, and the share of replicates that decrease and that increase |
| Per-pixel trend | The linear trend per decade is computed in each replicate; the same seven layers |
| Species index | The area mean (i.e., within Germany) is computed in each replicate, then the index and its percentiles |
| Combined indices | SBI and Chain are computed inside each replicate from replicate b of every species (the resamples are drawn independently for each species, so b is a shared number and not a shared resample); the MSI uses the standard deviation of each species index across replicates |
| Expected richness, community change, turnover | Computed in each replicate; five or seven layers as for the maps |
| Regional index (10, 20, 50 km) | Cell means, index and combination computed in each replicate on the raw grid; interval per cell and year, change and trend with shares of replicates decreasing and increasing, and a coverage layer; replicate 0 checked against the baseline regional index |

**What is not covered.** Errors in the environmental layers; the tuning of model settings (the number of trees included); survey-design bias and spatial or temporal dependence beyond what the blocks capture; the randomness of the thinning of the records; and the hindcast assumption (section 8). The models use the presence or absence of a detection, so a change in detectability or in survey effort over the years would enter the index as a change in habitat. Sampling error that species share (the same routes, years and observers) is not carried into the combined indices, because the species are resampled independently; we do not know whether this widens or narrows their interval. The climate scale has only about 13 blocks for Europe, so its resampling is coarse.

**A caveat for Perdix perdix.** In the BRT-only run, 9 of the 50 replicates of Perdix perdix have an index of exactly 100 in every year: in these resamples the meta-model found no usable signal, so the map of that replicate does not change over time. We kept these replicates in the interval, because a bootstrap has to repeat the main procedure, so the upper end of the Perdix interval (100) comes from them. A second interval without these replicates is planned for after the Steering Consortium meeting (improvements.md, item 17). Perdix perdix is not in the roster of the first version of the Monitor. Nothing in the pipeline detects replicates with a constant map, so whether one of the 14 species shows the same has to be checked in the v3 replicates.

**Reading the numbers.** The mean over replicates is not the baseline map; the baseline map is the point estimate and the replicates describe its uncertainty. With 25 replicates, the 5th and 95th percentiles each lie between the second and third most extreme replicate and are noisy; the 90% coverage is only nominal. The shares of replicates decreasing or increasing are shares, not probabilities, and have no threshold: a change of -0.0001 counts as a decrease. With 25 replicates they come in steps of 0.04. The first version of the Monitor has 25 replicates; more can be added if time allows.

## 8. Important information

**Five cautions for every number.**

1. **Hindcast.** The habitat scale is trained on 2022-2025 only. The maps for 2005-2021 apply that model to older layers, so they show how the landscape changed under fixed habitat preferences, not how the birds changed. Intervals do not include this assumption.
2. **Model uncertainty only.** The intervals describe sensitivity to the training data. They are not prediction intervals for counts in the field, and they do not cover errors in the environmental layers, model tuning or survey bias.
3. **Probabilities, not counts.** Indices are ratios of mean probabilities of occurrence and cannot be compared one-to-one with TRIM indices of counts.
4. **Few replicates.** The tails of percentile intervals from 25 replicates (50 in the BRT-only run of 12 October) are noisy; replicates can be added without changing the earlier ones.
5. **Thresholds are judgement calls.** The 0.05 limit for increase and decrease, the presence threshold of the binary maps and the floor of the regional index are stated choices, not estimates.

## 9. Changes since 12 October (they apply from the clean run for the first version of the Monitor)

I made these changes after the runs described above. None of them has been run yet on the full data; the results above do not contain them.

1. **One study area for all inputs.** The study area is defined once (a country, a region or a shapefile). Predictor layers are cropped and masked to it when they are made, with a buffer of 1 km for the records and the habitat and landscape layers and one 50 km cell for the climate predictions. The climate model is still fitted on all of Europe. Records are filtered to the area for every response, including the landscape scale. The final maps are still cut to the reporting area, so the Germany-only copies remain.
2. **Predictor layers are complete by construction.** Land cover has seven CORINE classes plus a residual class for cells with no mapped class. The landscape heterogeneity index no longer uses a 5% threshold: it is 0 where no class is mapped, so no cell inside the area is missing. Version 1 had left about 3% of the records of all species without a value and dropped them. A hard check stops the run if any layer has a missing value inside the area. The hedge layer is one fixed layer, the mean of the hedge layers of all years with data (decided on 3 November; the first plan, to copy the nearest earlier year, is not used), in the files of every year.
3. **DDA territory data.** A value of -1 in the territory count means that the species was present but not counted. It now counts as a presence (636 rows of the file).
4. **Species.** The roster has 14 species: Perdix perdix is out; Curruca communis (formerly Sylvia communis), Passer montanus, Motacilla flava and Falco tinnunculus are in. Falco tinnunculus is on trial: the layers do not resolve small woodlots, and it may not stay in the Monitor. The EBBA2 file now has 17 species; the climate scale takes the surveyed cells from the cells present in that file, so the absences of all species come from a universe that grew with the new species (section 2).
5. **Richness for every year.** The expected richness and its interval are computed for every mapped year, not only for 2025.
6. **National trend.** In the Monitor the national trend shows the period after the last published national indicator year as a dashed, preliminary line; the maps, the regional index and the per-species products use all the data. The cut-off year is not confirmed yet; the value in the settings is 2023, a placeholder.
7. **Land use.** The crop-type layers come from the HCTM map for every year up to 2023. For 2024 and 2025, where only the CTM map exists, its class shares are converted to the shares HCTM would have mapped, with a matrix fitted on the years 2017-2021. This is meant to remove the jumps in the country means of 2017, 2022 and 2024 that the earlier mixture of the two products produced; the continuity check on the v3 layers has to confirm it. The conversion cannot be checked directly for 2024 and 2025, because HCTM and this version of CTM do not overlap in any year. It removes the systematic difference between the products at the national level, not their local disagreement. Hedges are not part of the conversion (item 2).
8. **The run.** The first version of the Monitor is one run of the big 5 for 14 species, with 25 replicates and 90% intervals (5th to 95th percentile), and no BRT-only run with intervals. The habitat scale is trained on 2022-2025, so 2005-2021 are hindcasts. The numbers in sections 3 to 7 that come from the 11-species runs of October are marked as such and are replaced when the results of the clean run exist.
